list.listitem: Diagnosis should be made clinically through history and the presence of Bassett's sign, (tenderness along medial retinaculum) and/or hemarthrosis. A positive apprehension test can help confirm the diagnosis but is less sensitive. C
Evaluation should include imaging for osteochondral fracture, loose bodies, and other ligamentous injuries that may necessitate surgical intervention. C
Non-operative therapy is a good option and should include immediate short-term immobilization for comfort and subsequent initiation of physical therapy. B
Operative management is superior in terms of preventing redislocation at least in the short-term, but evidence is less robust for long-term benefit.B
Re-dislocation is likely and patients may require surgical intervention for recurrent dislocations and pain related to patellar instability. C

background.definition: Dislocation of the patella is the displacement of the patella laterally out of the femoral groove.

list.listitem: 5.8 per 100,000 persons per year in general population.
29 per 100,00 persons per year in 10- to 17-year-olds.

Among 131 patients aged 10 to 18, patellar dislocations caused 37% of acute post traumatic knee effusions (anterior cruciate ligament tears and isolated meniscus tears represented 22% and 15% of the second and third most common injuries, respectively).
Dislocation of the patella comprises 2% to 3% of all knee injuries.
Dislocation of the patella is the second most common cause for knee hemarthrosis.
Trauma
Classically, the patella will dislocate laterally out of the femoral sulcus at the start of knee flexion, with the quadriceps acting as a lateralizing force.

Diagnosis is made when the patella is lateral to the femoral groove, or when there is a subjective history of the patella sliding out of place with positive Bassett's sign, positive apprehension test, and/or presence of hemarthrosis. C
MRI and plain films should be used to evaluate for other ligamentous pathology, osteochondral defects, and loose bodies. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Joint line tenderness, positive Apley and/or McMurray test

list.listitem: Patient will typically present with knee pain and hemarthrosis. History often will include report of patella dislocating laterally.

The physical examination should focus on palpation for medial knee tenderness, the apprehension test (apprehension of re-dislocation, pain, and quadriceps flexion when laterally directed force is applied to the patella), and evaluation for other knee pathology.

Diagnosis is made when the patella is lateral to the femoral sulcus, or when there is a supportive history with knee effusion, hemarthrosis, positive Bassett's sign (tenderness along medial retinaculum), and/or positive apprehension test.
The presence of knee effusion is 83% sensitive for acute patellar dislocation; a positive Bassett's sign is 70% sensitive and a positive apprehension sign is 39% sensitive.

Imaging should include anteroposterior extended knee weight-bearing films and a Mercer-Merchant view (45-degree flexion of both knees over table end, and a 30-degree from horizontal XR tube angle for imaging shot) to rule out osteochondral fractures. Lateral radiographs with the knee fully extended, when evaluated using the Maldague and Malghem classification scheme for misalignment, has a 98% sensitivity and 65% specificity for previous dislocation.
Ultrasound can be a useful and accurate tool in the evaluation of osteochondral and medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) lesions.
MRI is useful in evaluating osteochondral defects and damage to the MPFL.

In one study, 37.7% of 122 children and adolescents (aged 11-18) with acute patellofemoral dislocation had evidence of osteochrondral injury, and in 44% osteochondral injury was only detected on MRI (e.g., the plain x-rays was a false negative test). However the presence or absence of a osteochondral fracture did not alter the emergency department management of 80 children presenting with lateral patellar dislocation.
Aspiration of the hemarthrosis is helpful in facilitating the examination and for analgesia. The presence of lipid globules in the aspirate is suggestive of osteochondral fracture.
Always evaluate for concurrent traumatic knee pathology.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Initial therapy should include short-term immobilization, followed by patella-stabilizing orthotics and physical therapy.
Surgery should be considered if chronic redislocation or instability develops.
Large osteochondral defects should be repaired surgically, and foreign bodies should be removed. C
Conservative management, including brief immobilization, supportive bracing, range of motion exercises, and knee strengthening, is a good option for initial patellar dislocations. C
Operative management is superior in terms of preventing redislocation at least in the short-term, but evidence is less robust for long-term benefit.B
Symptomatic pain control, as necessary.
Drainage of hemarthrosis is useful for immediate pain relief.
Surgery is suggested for repair of large osteochondral defects.

A systematic review identified 10 small randomized trials with a total of 510 patients randomized to surgery versus nonsurgical management. Redislocation was significantly less likely with surgery at 24 to 44 months (7 studies, 335 patients, RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.25 - 0.66), and was also numerically less likely at 72 to 86 months (3 studies, 195 patients, RR 0.58, 0.29 - 1.15) and in adolescents (3 studies, 174 patients, RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.26 - 1.37). Function was also improved significantly more with surgery based on the Kujala score.
Arthroscopy is indicated for removal of loose bodies.
Lateral release surgeries and medial tissue repair surgeries have yet to show improved patient subjective-based outcomes following initial patellar dislocations.
Some evidence suggests that arthroscopic repair of the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) decreases redislocation.
There is also some evidence to suggest that repair of the MPFL may increase the likelihood of return to a previous level of activity.

A large case series of 224 patients at a single center found that pain during activity improved post-operatively, and that only 3% required revision. A poor outcome was more likely in older patients (>30 years), obese patients, those with cartilage injury, and women.
Nonoperative management is an acceptable treatment option for first-time patellar dislocations that are not associated with large osteochondral defects or loose bodies.
Referral is necessary when conservative management has failed and/or surgery is indicated.
Redislocation occurs in 15% to 44% of all patients. B

Among children and adolescents with acute patellofemoral dislocation, nonoperative treatment was successful 62% of the time, and predictors of recurrence included "skeletally immature patients" with trochlear dysplasia.

In a small German study of 20 patients, no differences were noted in operative vs conservative treatment of traumatic acute patellofemoral dislocation with regards to redislocation rates at 24 months, as well as patient responses to a standardized questionnaire (Kujala score). However, the power of this study to identify a true difference (if one existed) was small.
Most patients with patellar dislocation recover completely and regain their pre-injury level of activity. B
Surgery is only indicated for large osteochondral fragments (>15 mm) in acute patellar dislocations.

cell.label: Patient presenting with knee pain and a history and physical examination suspicious for patellar dislocation. Is patella present in femoral groove?
Evaluation with MRI, ultrasound, and/or plain films to evaluate for presence of osteochondral fracture and loose bodies. Is large osteochondral fracture (>15 mm) present?
Is there a loose body present?
Nonoperative therapy with patella stabilizing orthotic and progressive range of motion and strengthening exercises. Redislocation or continued symptomatic patellar instability?
Surgical evaluation for potential arthroscopic or open procedure.
With knee fully extended apply pressure on the lateral/posterior aspect of patella until it returns to femoral groove. (Anesthesia may be required.)
